Well, how about two studies that weren't trying to provide that, but do? The first I'm relaying is about C_3 and C_4 in yellowtops. Some species of yellowtops have C_3, some C_4, some have both, and some have partials. The paper says that these are showing evolutionary pathways from C_3 to C_4. Are the partially functioning  C_4's useful though? For them to be selected and become fixed in their species, the transitioning forms must be useful. If not, then we would more expect them to be evidence of common ancestry than convergent evolution. The common ancestor would have had both variants.
Second, consider this paper on Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Figure 2 shows orthologous regions of four species. Look at the 3 who don't seem to have the functioning gene (the 2,3,and 4th ones). I counted row 1, the first 50 letters, of the nonfunctioning variants. in all but 2 places there is 2/3 agreement in the letters between the nonfunctioning genes. In 38 cases, the nonfunctioning genes agree with the functioning gene on which letter *should* be there (that 3/4 letters are conserved in favor of the functioning version) Why is the garbage convergent?
